title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany
abstract: Abstract Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.

title: The Evolution of Hours Worked and the Gender Wage Gap: Evidence From Four Countries
authors: Daniele Checchi; Daniel Kreisman; Cecilia García-Peñalosa
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the contribution of the intensive margin of labor supply (hours worked above zero) to the gender wage gap over a long time‐horizon across four high‐income economies: France, Germany, the UK, and the US. We do so by bridging a recent literature on gender differences in high‐paying, high‐hour jobs with traditional wage gap decomposition methods. We first build a model in which firms offer two wage contracts—one that pays a fixed wage but allows workers to choose their preferred number of hours up to “full time,” and a second in which wages are determined by imperfectly observable productivity and can require working more than standard hours. The former includes part‐ and full‐time work, while the latter requires workers to supply long hours but allows them to earn a higher remuneration. We then decompose the hourly wage gap separately for part‐, full‐, and overtime workers to observe the relative contribution of sorting and remuneration across these “hours regimes” over time and across countries. We show that while female employment in overtime work has increased and the gender wage gap has decreased in most countries and hours regimes, this was not driven by increasing selection on observables but rather by a decline over time of the unexplained component of the wage gap—a pattern that holds for most countries and hours regimes. We conclude by considering the contribution of the institutional framework (unions, labor market flexibility, parental leaves) to these cross‐country differences.

title: Birds of a Feather Earn Together: Gender and Peer Effects at the Workplace
authors: Julián Messina; Anna Sanz‐de‐Galdeano; Anastasia Terskaya
abstract: Abstract Utilizing comprehensive administrative data from Brazil, we investigate the impact of peer effects on wages, considering both within-gender and cross-gender dynamics. Since the average productivity of both individuals and their peers is unobservable, we estimate these values using worker fixed effects while accounting for occupational and firm sorting. Our findings reveal that within-gender peer effects have approximately twice the influence of cross-gender peer effects on wages for both men and women. Furthermore, we observe a reduction in the disparity between these two types of peer effects in settings characterized by greater gender equality.

‘The More We Could Be Involved in Stuff, the More Effective It'd Be’: The Need for More Employer Involvement in Active Labour Market Policy
abstract: ABSTRACT While internationally, interest has grown in employer engagement with active labour market policy (ALMP), their involvement in policy development has been limited—especially in liberal market economies, which lack the institutional frameworks and traditions of social partnership observed elsewhere. Applying a social dialogue lens to interviews with 124 employers, policymakers and other social actors in the UK context, we consider its potential expressive and instrumental functions, and the extent to which facilitating conditions exist to enable it. As in‐work poverty and poor job quality present key intractable challenges for policymakers at national and local levels, we present a revival in social dialogue in ALM policymaking as a critical factor for preventing institutional failure and unlocking innovative policy solutions, especially where supporting people to access and progress in ‘good work’ is a policy priority.

title: The Teacher and the Test? an Analysis of the Short and Long‐Run Predictive Power of Achievement Indicators
authors: Lex Borghans; Ron Diris; Trudie Schils
abstract: ABSTRACT Test scores provide objective indicators of student achievement, but are argued to neglect certain skills. Teacher assessments, conversely, are subjective but typically designed to provide a more holistic evaluation of student potential. Combining survey and administrative data for the Netherlands, we estimate the predictive power of test scores and teacher assessments measured at age 12 across the life cycle, and analyse what this predictive power reflects. We find that the non‐overlapping predictive power of both indicators is strong. While the predictive power of the teacher assessment is partially driven by socio‐economic bias, self‐fulfilling prophecy effects and, especially, test measurement error, we find that it also captures productive skills that tests do not.
journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: The accuracy of jobseekers’ wage expectations
authors: Marco Caliendo; Robert Mahlstedt; Aiko Schmeißer
abstract: We study the accuracy of wage expectations among unemployed workers by comparing subjective beliefs to benchmark and realized wages using linked survey-administrative data. On average, jobseekers overestimate their reemployment wages, with optimism concentrated among those with low earnings potential. Beliefs are anchored to past wages, and inaccuracies persist over the course of unemployment and in response to stronger search incentives. Moreover, there is an asymmetry in belief formation: individuals who are likely to experience wage losses relative to their previous job are particularly rigid in adjusting their expectations. Finally, wage optimism predicts higher reservation wages, greater search intensity, and delayed reemployment.

title: Immigrants and the market for taxi drivers
abstract: Abstract Immigrants face many obstacles to labor market integration in developed countries, often clustering in certain lower-skilled occupations. To investigate the role of such occupations, this paper studies how labor market outcomes evolve after gaining access to a canonical immigrant occupation: taxi driving. Comparing individuals who choose to pursue and pass the necessary written examinations for a taxi driver’s license to both those who have not yet done so and those who never take taxi examinations, we find that non-Western immigrants increase their monthly earnings by nearly 50 percent between 1 and 3 years later. Moreover, reliance on social insurance programs drops substantially. Natives experience smaller benefits and appear to use taxi driving to recover from negative labor market shocks. We also find that immigrants remain in taxi driving over time and that recently arrived immigrants reap the largest benefits.
